title: Microorganisms in Food — General Characteristics, Classification and Morphology
shortDescription: Bacteria, yeasts, moulds, viruses and parasites: how they differ in structure, size and importance to food.
genZNote: Microbes are tiny, everywhere, and low-key running your kitchen. Gram +ve vs Gram −ve is their personality test.

table.caption: Microbial groups in food
rows: Bread, beer, wine; spoilage of juices and sugary foods
Norovirus, hepatitis A — need host; do not multiply in food

sections.heading: Bacterial Morphology
bullets: Shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rods), spirilla/vibrios (curved/spiral); arrangements: chains (Streptococcus), clusters (Staphylococcus), diplo.

Gram stain separates Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan; Staphylococcus, Bacillus, Clostridium, Listeria, Lactobacillus) from Gram-negative (outer membrane with LPS; Salmonella, E. coli, Vibrio, Pseudomonas).
Structures: cell wall, cytoplasmic membrane, flagella (motility), pili, capsule/slime, endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium — heat-resistant survival forms).
Fungal morphology: yeast buds; mould hyphae/mycelium with spores (conidia).

sections.heading: Classification and Nomenclature
bullets: Binomial nomenclature (Genus species); Bergey's Manual for bacteria.
Classified by morphology, Gram reaction, oxygen need (aerobe, anaerobe, facultative), temperature (psychrophile, mesophile, thermophile), nutrition and genetics (16S rRNA).
Food microbes are also grouped by role: spoilage, pathogenic, beneficial (starter, probiotic) and indicator organisms (coliforms, Enterobacteriaceae, E. coli).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Food microorganisms include bacteria, yeasts, moulds, viruses and parasites classified by structure, staining and physiology, and by their role as spoilers, pathogens or beneficial agents.
keyFacts: Gram +ve: thick peptidoglycan; Gram −ve: LPS outer membrane.
Viruses do not grow in food.

highYieldFacts: Endospores survive boiling; destroyed by autoclaving 121 °C.
commonTraps: Do not say viruses multiply in food.
